passage:
Counsellor's note, student wellbeing centre, 3 October.
Disha (20) booked the session for exam stress but spent most of it talking about her girlfriend, Mehak. Observations: she checked her phone four times. She described asking Mehak "Are we okay?" several times this week, and dropping hints like "Must be nice to have so much free time." She said she sounded sharper than she meant to, "like a tax officer". When I asked what she was afraid of, she was quiet, then said, "That one day she'll just stop replying." Her shoulders dropped as she said it. I reflected that the questions and hints seem to come from fear of being left rather than anger. Next step: she will try one direct sentence with Mehak, "I miss you and I'm worried about us." Follow-up in two weeks.

qa.q: How many times did Disha check her phone during the session?
qa.a: She checked her phone four times.

qa.q: What is Disha afraid of underneath the hints and questions?
qa.a: She is afraid Mehak will one day just stop replying, which is a fear of being left.

qa.q: What turning point does the counsellor suggest at this early stage?
qa.a: The counsellor suggests one direct, gentle sentence, "I miss you and I'm worried about us", instead of hints and a sharp tone.

qa.q: How might Mehak be experiencing the repeated "Are we okay?" questions?
qa.a: Mehak may feel tested or criticised by the hints, without knowing that fear, not anger, is behind them.

grounding: Shows a young woman who feels her relationship slipping, whose fear of being left comes out as questions, hints and a sharp tone.

passage:
Sunday night.
Gurpreet left after lunch and I've felt weird all evening. He was on his phone half the time, laughing at something he didn't show me. I asked, "Everything okay with us?" He said, "Obviously, Madhu. You're my girl. Why?" Then I asked again while he was putting on his shoes. He sighed. And as he left I said, "Say hi to your very interesting phone." I heard how it sounded. Snippy. Not me. What I actually wanted to say was: I feel like you're drifting, and I'm scared I'm not enough anymore. Why can't I just say that? Instead it leaks out sideways, in questions and little jabs. Tomorrow I'll try. Maybe.
— Madhuri

qa.q: What did Madhuri say to Gurpreet as he left?
qa.a: She said, "Say hi to your very interesting phone."

qa.q: What did Madhuri actually want to tell Gurpreet?
qa.a: She wanted to say that she feels him drifting and is scared she isn't enough anymore. 😟

qa.q: What could Madhuri try tomorrow?
qa.a: She could say the real feeling directly and gently, "I feel you drifting and I'm scared", instead of questions and jabs.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet have taken the repeated question and the jab?
qa.a: Gurpreet may have felt checked on and needled, sighing because he doesn't see the fear underneath it.

grounding: Shows a young woman craving reassurance whose fear of losing her partner leaks out as repeated questions and a sharper tone than she means.

passage:
Kishore had been checking his phone every few minutes since six. Vidya had replied to his long message with just "haha ya."
They'd been together two years. Lately she was busy with her internship in Andheri, tired on calls, and he felt like he was talking to the back of her head.
When she finally called at ten, he said, "So. Are you even happy with us?" It came out sharper than he meant.
"What? Where is this coming from?"
"Nothing. Just, you seem busy."
He wanted her to say she missed him. He wanted a proper talk. What he was really scared of, he didn't say: that she was slowly leaving.

qa.q: How did Vidya reply to Kishore's long message?
qa.a: She replied with just "haha ya."

qa.q: What was Kishore really afraid of underneath his sharp question?
qa.a: He was scared that Vidya was slowly leaving him, and he felt anxious and lonely because she seemed busy and distant.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Kishore at this early stage?
qa.a: He could say directly that he misses her and feels a bit scared, instead of hinting with sharp questions.

qa.q: What might Vidya be experiencing when Kishore asks if she's happy?
qa.a: She seems caught off guard and confused, maybe feeling accused while she is just tired from her internship.

grounding: A young man feels his relationship slipping and craves reassurance, but his fear of being left comes out as a sharp question and hints.

passage:
"Did you eat?" Sachin asked.
"Yes," said Ankita, not looking up from her laptop.
"What did you eat?"
"Dal rice. Why?"
"Just asking. You didn't reply all afternoon."
"I was in class, Sachin."
"Right. Class." He sat on the edge of the hostel visitor bench. "You used to text from class."
Ankita finally looked up. "What's going on?"
"Nothing. Forget it." He rubbed the back of his neck. "It's just… are we okay?"
"Why wouldn't we be?"
Sachin didn't know how to say it. That she felt far away. That he needed her to say she wasn't going anywhere.

qa.q: What did Ankita say she ate?
qa.a: Dal rice.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling underneath his questions?
qa.a: He felt insecure and afraid that Ankita was drifting away, and he needed reassurance but couldn't say it plainly.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Sachin here?
qa.a: He could name his real need, for example "I've been feeling far from you and I'm scared," instead of asking small questions that sound like checking.

qa.q: What might Ankita be experiencing as the questions continue?
qa.a: She may feel puzzled and a bit checked on, not understanding why simple questions about lunch feel so heavy.

grounding: A young man senses his relationship slipping and craves reassurance, but it comes out as questions and hints rather than his real fear.

passage:
Looking back at that winter, I can see what was happening better than I could then.
Sabina had started a new job at the bookstore, and suddenly weekends were full. I told myself I was fine. But I kept asking little things. "Who's that friend you mentioned?" "Are you coming Sunday or not?" My tone got sharp, and she'd look at me like I was a stranger.
What I really wanted was a proper talk, just sitting together and hearing that we were okay. Underneath all the questions, I was scared she was already halfway out the door.
I didn't say that. I said, "Fine, do what you want." I'm Eshaan, and I wish I'd said the scary part.

qa.q: Where had Sabina started a new job?
qa.a: At the bookstore.

qa.q: What was Eshaan feeling underneath all the small questions?
qa.a: Eshaan was scared that Sabina was already halfway out the door and anxious for reassurance.

qa.q: What turning point was available to Eshaan that winter?
qa.a: Eshaan could have asked for a proper talk and said the scary part plainly, instead of sharp questions and "Fine, do what you want."

qa.q: What might Sabina have been experiencing that winter?
qa.a: She was likely busy and confused by the sharp tone, feeling questioned rather than wanted.

grounding: Looking back, a young adult sees how fear of being left came out as sharp questions and hints instead of asking for a proper talk.

passage:
Counselling centre, student session note, Tuesday.

Darshan, a second-year student, came in saying he "just needed to vent." Over forty minutes, a pattern emerged. His girlfriend, Indu, has been busy with her theatre rehearsals for six weeks, and they talk less.

He described checking when she was last online, sending "Everything okay with us?" at midnight, and hinting that "some people make time." He said his tone has been sharper than he intends. When asked what he was most afraid of, he was quiet, then said, "That she'll get bored of me and I'll be the last to know."

I noted the fear of being left sitting under the questions and hints. Next step agreed: before our next session, he will try one direct, calm sentence to Indu about what he misses, instead of a hint. We'll look at how it went on Friday.

qa.q: How long has Indu been busy with theatre rehearsals?
qa.a: She has been busy for six weeks.

qa.q: What is Darshan most afraid of?
qa.a: He is afraid Indu will get bored of him and leave, and that he will be the last to know.

qa.q: Why is one calm, direct sentence a useful next step?
qa.a: It lets Darshan ask for what he really needs, closeness and reassurance, without the hints and sharp tone that could push Indu away.

qa.q: How might Indu be experiencing Darshan's midnight messages?
qa.a: Indu may feel pressured or confused by the hints and sharp tone, unaware of the fear of being left that lies under them.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a young man craving reassurance, with fear of being left coming out as questions, hints and a sharper tone.
